deepDiveH2: Why do special characters sometimes look broken on other sites?
deepDiveP: Like emoji, special characters are standard Unicode text — but unlike emoji, most are plain black-and-white glyphs, so they're less affected by font differences. Still, older systems or certain programs that don't support a given character may show a box (□) or question mark instead. A character that pastes fine into a word processor can still break in an old forum or a code environment using a legacy encoding like EUC-KR, so it's worth checking in the actual place you plan to use it.
deepDiveList: × (multiplication sign, U+00D7) vs. x (the letter X) — often confused in formulas or product names because they look nearly identical
– (en dash) vs. — (em dash) vs. - (hyphen) — each has a different use in a sentence
Curly quotes (' ') vs. straight quotes (" ") — word processors auto-convert to curly quotes, but code usually needs straight quotes

faq.q: Are these symbols free to use?
faq.a: Yes. Every character here is a standard Unicode text character, so it isn't subject to copyright and can be used freely.

faq.q: Can I search in other languages?
faq.a: Yes. You can search character names in English, Korean, Japanese, or Chinese.

faq.q: Do I need to sign up?
faq.a: No. You can search and copy symbols immediately, no account required.

faq.q: A character I copied looks broken in another program
faq.a: This usually means that program or font doesn't support the Unicode character. Try switching fonts or checking that your app is up to date.

faq.q: Do I need HTML entity codes to use these in a webpage?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Most modern webpages use UTF-8 encoding, so pasting the character directly usually displays correctly.
